title: Intermolecular Forces
seo_title: Grade 11 Physical Sciences: Intermolecular Forces Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_text: Intermolecular forces: London (dispersion) forces, dipole–dipole forces, ion–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds; the effect of intermolecular forces on melting point, boiling point, vapour pressure, viscosity, solubility and surface tension; the unique properties of water. (summary of CAPS Physical Sciences, Grade 11, Chemistry: Intermolecular forces)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Physical Sciences worksheets (CAPS): London forces, dipole–dipole forces, hydrogen bonds, physical properties and the properties of water. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Stronger intermolecular forces mean a higher boiling point.
key_sub: Hydrogen bonds form when H is bonded to N, O or F.
body_html:
How to think about it

Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules; they are much weaker than the covalent bonds inside molecules. London forces act between all molecules and are larger for bigger molecules; dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules; hydrogen bonds are strong dipole–dipole forces between molecules with H bonded to N, O or F.

The stronger the intermolecular forces, the higher the melting point, boiling point and viscosity, and the lower the vapour pressure. Water has hydrogen bonds, so it has a high boiling point for its size, a high specific heat and high surface tension, and ice is less dense than liquid water.

Example

Which has the higher boiling point, H₂O or H₂S?

Hydrogen bonding

Answer: H₂O

Example

Why does iodine dissolve in hexane but not in water?

Like dissolves like.

Answer: both are non-polar

Common mistakes

  • Thinking boiling breaks covalent bonds.
  • Thinking hydrogen bonds are bonds inside a molecule.
  • Thinking higher vapour pressure means stronger forces.

items.q: What is electronegativity?
c: the power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond
the number of bonds an atom forms
the energy to remove an electron
items.e: Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

items.q: What is the bond angle in H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2,5°.

items.q: Why does magnesium have a higher melting point than sodium?
c: Mg²⁺ has a larger charge and there are more delocalised electrons
items.e: Stronger metallic bonding.

items.q: Which substance has hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
items.e: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F.

items.q: Which substance conducts electricity when molten but not when solid?
items.e: Ions are fixed in the solid but free to move when molten.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of hydrogen sulfide (H<sub>2</sub>S)?

items.e: Polar molecules without H bonded to N, O or F have dipole-dipole forces.

items.q: What is the bond angle in XeF<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2,5°.

items.e: Nonpolar particles only have intermolecular forces.

items.q: Why does diamond have a very high melting point?
c: many strong covalent bonds must be broken
items.e: Diamond is a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure.

items.q: Why is water's boiling point (100 °C) much higher than that of H₂S (−60 °C)?

items.e: H₂S has only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.

items.q: Why is CO₂ a non-polar molecule even though its C=O bonds are polar?
c: carbon and oxygen have the same electronegativity
it is linear, so the bond dipoles cancel
items.e: Molecular shape decides overall polarity.

items.q: Why do the boiling points of the noble gases increase down the group?
c: there are more electrons, so van der Waals forces are stronger
items.e: Bigger atoms have bigger induced dipole–dipole forces.

items.q: What is the strongest type of intermolecular force?
items.e: Covalent bonds are within molecules, not between them.
